stories.title: Rescue Teams Save Woman After 36 Hours Trapped in Colombia Earthquake Rubble
stories.summary: A 32-year-old woman was rescued alive after being trapped for 36 hours under the rubble of a collapsed building in Pereira, Colombia, following a 7.4-magnitude earthquake. Rescuers located her 10 hours before successfully reaching her, as they continue to search for more survivors amid the devastation.

explore_lenses.label: Why did the rescue take so long?
explore_lenses.title: Deep debris made extraction hazardous
explore_lenses.summary: The reported 10-hour gap between locating Daniela Largo Sánchez and freeing her reflects the risks of moving through unstable collapsed material, not simply a delay in finding her.

claims.text: Bogotá firefighters said crews located Largo Sánchez about 10 hours before her rescue but could not immediately extract her because she was buried too deeply.
Firefighters said they worked carefully through the debris to reach her without causing another collapse, illustrating the tradeoff between speed and rescuer/survivor safety.
Aid agencies regard the first 48 to 72 hours after a collapse as especially important for finding people alive, although survival can extend beyond that when trapped people have food and water.

explore_lenses.label: How severe is the wider emergency?
explore_lenses.title: Rescue figures and missing counts are still moving
explore_lenses.summary: The individual rescue occurred within a much larger disaster across western Colombia, but the true number of people missing and the eventual casualty total remained unsettled as of August 12.

claims.text: President Abelardo de la Espriella said by Tuesday that the magnitude 7.4 quake had killed at least 181 people and injured 2,595 in western Colombia.
The president put the number of missing people at at least 195, while civilian-run databases listed nearly 4,000; the gap reflects incomplete information rather than competing confirmed totals.
Deaths and major damage were reported in Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdó, while local leaders and families voiced concern that rural-area impacts were still poorly documented.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after the rescue phase?
explore_lenses.title: Aid and recovery operations are expanding
explore_lenses.summary: Authorities are pairing the immediate search with emergency financing and outside assistance, while humanitarian organizations say the earthquake has compounded needs in areas already affected by displacement and armed conflict.

claims.text: The government declared an emergency to speed funding for recovery after initial assessments found roughly 1,600 damaged buildings, including at least 61 that had completely collapsed.
Giovanni Rizzo, Colombia director for the Norwegian Refugee Council, said the quake compounds an already severe humanitarian situation and requires greater support for the response.

María José Torres, the U.N. resident coordinator in Colombia, said aid organizations already operating in conflict-affected areas, including Chocó near the epicenter, have increased capacity to be present with affected communities.
The United States offered more than $15 million in assistance, while Mexico and El Salvador said they planned to send personnel, supplies or aid shipments.

story_report.summary: A 32-year-old woman was pulled alive from the rubble of a collapsed building 36 hours after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia. Rescue crews had located her about 10 hours earlier but needed time to reach her safely. By Tuesday, President Abelardo de la Espriella said the quake had killed at least 181 people and injured 2,595, leaving emergency teams to contend with widespread destruction and an uncertain number of missing people.

sections.heading: Rescue Crews Navigate Collapse Risks
sections.body: Bogotá firefighters said the woman, identified as Largo Sánchez, was buried too deeply for an immediate extraction after crews found her. Firefighters worked cautiously through the debris to avoid triggering another collapse, balancing the urgency of the rescue against the safety of both the survivor and responders. Aid agencies consider the first 48 to 72 hours after a building collapse especially important for finding survivors, though people can live longer when they have access to food and water.

sections.heading: Earthquake Damage Spans Western Colombia
sections.body: Deaths and major damage were reported in Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdó, while local leaders and families said the effects in rural areas remained poorly documented. The government’s initial assessment found about 1,600 damaged buildings, including at least 61 that had completely collapsed. The president put the number of missing people at at least 195, while civilian-run databases listed nearly 4,000, a gap attributed to incomplete information rather than competing confirmed totals.

sections.heading: Emergency Declaration Speeds Recovery Funding
sections.body: The government declared an emergency to accelerate funding for recovery. Giovanni Rizzo, Colombia director for the Norwegian Refugee Council, said the quake had compounded an already severe humanitarian situation and required greater support. María José Torres, the U.N. resident coordinator, said organizations working in conflict-affected areas, including Chocó near the epicenter, had expanded their capacity; the United States offered more than $15 million in assistance, while Mexico and El Salvador planned aid shipments, supplies or personnel.

stories.title: David Crowley Wins Wisconsin Democratic Primary, Set to Face Tom Tiffany
stories.summary: David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, has won the Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor, defeating progressive candidate Francesca Hong. Crowley, who was backed by Governor Tony Evers, will face Republican Representative Tom Tiffany in the upcoming November election. This victory marks a notable shift in the Democratic primary landscape, as Crowley represents a more moderate stance compared to Hong's democratic socialist platform.

explore_lenses.label: Why did Evers and allied groups back Crowley?
explore_lenses.title: A coalition-and-experience case
explore_lenses.summary: Crowley’s supporters emphasized his executive record and their belief that he could unite Democratic strongholds with voters elsewhere in Wisconsin. Those are stakeholder arguments, not proof of general-election performance.

claims.text: Crowley’s campaign said his Milwaukee County record included affordable-housing expansion, public-health and public-safety investment, tax relief, and support for Act 12, the bipartisan local-government finance law.
Crowley argued that Democrats need turnout in Milwaukee and Madison while remaining competitive in suburban and rural areas; he presented that as the path to defeating Tiffany.
Evers, U.S. Rep. Gwen Moore, several building-trades and firefighter unions, and Black Leaders Organizing Communities were listed as Crowley endorsers.

explore_lenses.title: Competing governing priorities
explore_lenses.summary: The general election will feature contrasting campaign claims about government management, affordability, taxes and regulation. The candidates’ own sites describe priorities, but do not establish that their proposals would achieve the stated results.

claims.text: Crowley says his governing approach centers on managing government, working across differences and building consensus, and he presents affordable housing, public health, public safety and tax relief as parts of his record.
Tiffany’s campaign has highlighted housing supply, regulatory costs, property taxes and limits on institutional ownership of homes in its homeownership agenda.
Tiffany’s campaign also frames tax policy as a central contrast, calling for an end to what it describes as Evers-era tax increases; that is the campaign’s characterization.

explore_lenses.title: Certification first, then the general election
explore_lenses.summary: Crowley’s apparent primary victory makes him the Democratic nominee in reporting, but Wisconsin’s election-night totals are unofficial until the statutory canvass and certification process is completed. The next statewide contest is the November 3 general election.

claims.text: Wisconsin’s election authority says election-night results are unofficial and that certification proceeds through municipal, county and then state levels.
AP reported that a delay involving about 28,000 Milwaukee absentee ballots stemmed from a data-uploading error, contributing to the late resolution of the close primary.
Wisconsin’s official ballot-access materials identify the 2026 general election date as November 3, 2026.

stories.summary: A Syrian court has sentenced former president Bashar al-Assad and his brother Maher to death in absentia for war crimes and crimes against humanity related to the civil war. The court's decision comes after both men were found responsible for their actions in the conflict, which has resulted in approximately 500,000 deaths. The two brothers are currently believed to be in Moscow.

explore_lenses.label: Why does this verdict matter for Syria?
explore_lenses.title: A landmark test of transitional justice
explore_lenses.summary: The ruling is the first against Bashar al-Assad or his inner circle since the family’s rule ended, making it a major symbolic accountability step. It also tests whether Syria’s new institutions can deliver justice viewed as lawful, inclusive and credible.

claims.text: The Damascus verdicts are the first against Assad or members of his inner circle since the former ruling family lost power in December 2024.
Victims’ lawyer Adnan al-Masalmeh described the ruling as justice for people killed, detained, wounded or displaced under the former government.

Human Rights Watch says Syria’s domestic legal framework does not expressly criminalize war crimes or crimes against humanity, lacks command-responsibility provisions, and retains capital punishment—gaps it says raise questions about how such prosecutions will work in practice.

story_report.summary: A Syrian court in Damascus has sentenced former president Bashar al-Assad and his brother Maher to death in absentia after finding them responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity during Syria’s civil war, which killed about 500,000 people. sections.heading: First Damascus verdicts after Assad fall

His assessment reflects the perspective of victims’ representatives rather than a finding on the proceedings’ broader legal legitimacy.

sections.heading: Human Rights Watch cites legal gaps
sections.body: Human Rights Watch says Syria’s domestic legal framework does not expressly criminalize war crimes or crimes against humanity and does not include command-responsibility provisions. The group also notes that capital punishment remains in force, arguing that these gaps raise practical questions about how such prosecutions can proceed. The organization’s assessment is a critique of the legal framework, not a determination that the court’s verdict is invalid.

sections.heading: UN plans transitional justice support

explore_lenses.summary: Zhu Rongji’s tenure is associated with reforms that made China’s economy more market-oriented while retaining state control over key sectors. The gains in growth and trade came with disruptive costs, particularly from restructuring state industry.

explore_lenses.label: Why does the WTO date matter?
explore_lenses.title: China joined in 2001, not 2002
explore_lenses.summary: Zhu was a central political figure in the final accession push, but China formally became a WTO member on December 11, 2001. The accession locked in commitments to open parts of the economy and became a major marker of China’s global economic integration.

claims.text: The WTO approved China’s accession terms on November 10, 2001; China became the organization’s 143rd member on December 11, 2001 after depositing its instrument of ratification.
The accession package included commitments to open and liberalize China’s trade regime and to provide a more predictable environment for trade and foreign investment under WTO rules.

In 2021, WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala described China’s accession as pivotal and said integration-supported growth benefited China and trading partners; she also noted that some WTO members wanted China to do more on WTO reform, level-playing-field issues and dispute settlement.
A World Bank analysis estimated large gains from China’s pre-accession and post-accession trade reforms, while warning that benefits and adjustment costs would differ across sectors and workers.

sections.heading: Zhu Rongji’s Economic Reform Record
sections.body: As vice premier and premier, Zhu pushed measures to cool economic overheating in the early 1990s, centralize more tax revenue, restructure or close many state enterprises, and advance housing-ownership reforms. sections.heading: China’s WTO Entry and Legacy
sections.body: China’s WTO accession terms were approved on Nov. 10, 2001, and the country became the organization’s 143rd member on Dec. 11, 2001 after depositing its ratification instrument. The package committed China to opening and liberalizing its trade regime and to providing a more predictable setting for trade and foreign investment under WTO rules. In 2021, WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala called accession pivotal, while noting calls from some members for further action on WTO reform, level-playing-field issues and dispute settlement.

sections.heading: China’s Reform Challenges Continue
sections.body: Zhu served as premier until early 2003. The bank projected 4.4% growth for 2026, identifying property-sector adjustment, soft labor conditions and trade-policy uncertainty as risks, and said stronger social protection and a more predictable business environment could support confidence.

explore_lenses.label: What happens next in South Carolina’s Senate race?
explore_lenses.title: Graham and Norman move to an August 25 Republican runoff
explore_lenses.summary: The August 11 vote narrowed South Carolina’s special Republican Senate primary to Darline Graham and Ralph Norman; the runoff winner will become the party’s nominee for the November special election.

claims.text: Darline Graham and Ralph Norman emerged from a 10-candidate Republican field to advance to the August 25 runoff for the seat formerly held by Graham’s late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham.

Graham credited Trump’s endorsement and said she would support his agenda; Norman’s campaign emphasized his congressional experience, while Democratic nominee Annie Andrews said her campaign would focus on affordability and health care.
AP forecast that the August 25 Republican runoff winner is expected to win the Senate seat over the Democratic nominee in the November special election.

The South Carolina Election Commission said voters who participated in the June Democratic primary could not vote in the August 11 special Republican primary, while June Republican-primary voters and voters who skipped both June primaries could participate.

story_report.summary: Voters cast ballots in primaries across Wisconsin, Minnesota, Alabama, Connecticut, Vermont and South Carolina on Aug. 11. Key races produced divergent results for candidates backed by President Donald Trump, while a Wisconsin Democratic contest remained unsettled because of a ballot-data handling problem. In South Carolina, Darline Graham and Ralph Norman advanced to a Republican Senate runoff scheduled for Aug. 25, setting up the next decision in a special-election race.

sections.heading: Wisconsin Democratic Contest Remains Uncalled

Francesca Hong and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley was too early to call after Milwaukee officials said audit logs, rather than ballot results, were uploaded to flash drives. Crowley, endorsed by outgoing Democratic Gov. Tony Evers, presented himself as the more moderate candidate; Hong identifies as a democratic socialist. Election-night totals in Wisconsin remain unofficial pending municipal and county canvasses and state certification.

sections.heading: South Carolina Senate Runoff Approaches
sections.body: Graham and Norman emerged from a 10-candidate Republican field seeking the seat formerly held by Graham's late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham. Graham credited Trump's endorsement and said she would support his agenda, while Norman emphasized his congressional experience; Democratic nominee Annie Andrews said she would focus on affordability and health care. The Associated Press forecast that the Republican runoff winner would be expected to defeat Andrews in November's special election.

sections.heading: South Carolina Primary Eligibility Rules
sections.body: South Carolina election officials said voters who participated in the June Democratic primary could not vote in the Aug. 11 special Republican primary. Those who voted in the June Republican primary, as well as voters who skipped both June primaries, were eligible to take part.

explore_lenses.title: Renewed attacks have widened the immediate danger
explore_lenses.summary: The reported deaths come amid a renewed period of attacks and threats against commercial traffic in the Red Sea. International maritime authorities say the danger extends beyond individual ships to crews, trade routes and potential pollution.

claims.text: The International Maritime Organization said on July 23 that the latest reported Red Sea attacks endangered seafarers, international shipping, the marine environment and global supply chains.

The IMO Secretary-General called de-escalation the only solution; this is a policy appeal, not confirmation that attacks will stop.

explore_lenses.label: How did attacks reach this point?
explore_lenses.title: A long-running campaign has repeatedly hit merchant shipping
explore_lenses.summary: The incident follows a multi-year Houthi campaign against vessels in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. UN reporting documents a gap between the group's stated targeting rationale and the vessels actually affected.

claims.text: A UN Panel of Experts reported at least 134 attacks from Houthi-controlled areas against merchant or commercial vessels and U.S. or U.K. warships between November 15, 2023 and July 31, 2024.
The Panel found that, despite Houthi claims they would target Israeli-linked vessels, the attacks had indiscriminately affected vessels navigating in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

The UN Secretary-General said the July 2025 sinking of the Magic Seas and Eternity C, with deaths, injuries and missing crew, represented a dangerous re-escalation; an IMO incident report then listed three confirmed fatalities from the Eternity C attack during search-and-rescue operations.

story_report.summary: A Houthi attack on a vessel killed six people, including three Pakistani nationals, according to reports cited in the evidence packet. The deaths add to risks faced by crews and commercial shipping in the Red Sea region, where the International Maritime Organization has warned that recent attacks endanger seafarers, shipping, the marine environment and global supply chains. Pakistan has described hostile acts against its vessels or maritime interests as a grave national-security threat and said it reserves the right to take self-defence measures consistent with international law.

sections.heading: Red Sea Attack Record
sections.body: A UN panel documented at least 134 attacks launched from Houthi-controlled areas against merchant or commercial vessels and U.S. or British warships between Nov. 15, 2023, and July 31, 2024. The panel said the attacks indiscriminately affected vessels navigating the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, despite Houthi statements that Israeli-linked shipping was their target. In July 2025, the UN secretary-general described the sinkings of the Magic Seas and Eternity C, which caused deaths, injuries and missing crew, as a dangerous re-escalation.

sections.heading: Maritime Security Responses
sections.body: The IMO has urged ship operators to assess transit risks and called for de-escalation, while its secretary-general said de-escalation was the only solution. The organization did not announce an escort arrangement, route reopening or other operational measure. Separately, U.S. Central Command said it disabled the Botswana-flagged tanker M/T Lexie on June 2 after it ignored warnings while heading toward Kharg Island, Iran, describing the action as part of a U.S. blockade of traffic entering and leaving Iranian ports.

unresolved.text: The consulted official material does not identify the vessel attacked, its flag, the weapon used, or the names and nationalities of all six people reported killed.
The reviewed sources do not establish whether the Houthis publicly claimed responsibility for this specific attack or whether the vessel fell within a declared Houthi targeting category.

highlights.title: Ebola Outbreak in Congo Claims Over 2,000 Lives, Marked as Fastest Growing on Record
highlights.summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo reports that at least 2,000 people have died in its ongoing Ebola outbreak, which is now recognized as the fastest growing on record. The outbreak reportedly began months before it was officially declared in May, complicating response efforts due to factors such as rebel conflict and infrastructure challenges.

stories.title: Deadly Earthquake Strikes Colombia, Causing Widespread Destruction
stories.summary: A powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, resulting in at least 132 fatalities and over 570 injuries. The quake, described as the country's strongest in years, led to significant destruction, with many buildings collapsing and rescue efforts underway to find survivors. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a state of emergency shortly after taking office, and the European Union is providing support for rescue operations.

explore_lenses.summary: The response must cover damaged cities as well as the remote Chocó area near the epicenter. Communications and transport constraints may delay confirmation of casualties and delivery of rescue resources.

President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a state of emergency to speed recovery funding as authorities confronted widespread destruction across several cities. sections.heading: Remote Chocó Complicates Damage Assessment
sections.body: Near the epicenter, San José del Palmar is in mountainous Chocó and has no airport, while parts of the regional capital, Quibdó, lost phone service after the quake. Much of Chocó can be reached only by boat or plane, complicating assessments beyond major cities. Hundreds of buildings were damaged or destroyed across Cali, Pereira, Quibdó and Manizales, requiring rescue teams to work at multiple urban sites.

sections.heading: Emergency Response Expands Across Colombia
sections.body: De la Espriella suspended planned travel and convened a Unified Command Post at the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management and the National Disaster Management Committee. Authorities suspended flights at six airports while damage was assessed, and hospitals in five cities were placed on red alert. The mayors of Pereira and Cali said curfews were intended to prevent looting and help relief operations; the European Commission mobilized Copernicus satellite services for rescue support.

It remained unclear how many damaged buildings were unsafe, how long transport disruptions would last, whether more victims would be found, and how emergency recovery funds would be allocated or when they would be distributed.

explore_lenses.label: Why does this verdict matter for Syrian justice?
explore_lenses.title: A first domestic judgment against Assad-era leaders
explore_lenses.summary: The ruling is significant chiefly as Syria's first conviction of Bashar al-Assad or members of his inner circle since the former government fell, creating a domestic judicial record of alleged state crimes. Its practical value also depends on whether the proceedings meet fair-trial standards and broaden accountability beyond the former government.

claims.text: The Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus sentenced Bashar al-Assad and Maher al-Assad in absentia, while Atef Najib was tried in person; reporting described the decision as the first Syrian conviction against Assad or his inner circle.

The case grew from the first public national criminal proceedings against a senior Assad-era security figure, with 50 civil plaintiffs listed during the opening sessions, according to trial monitoring by the Syrian Network for Human Rights.

Amnesty International says the National Commission for Transitional Justice was initially mandated to address serious violations by the former Assad government, while the commission told Amnesty that proposed legislation would extend to abuses by all conflict parties.

Amnesty identifies continuing institutional concerns: judicial appointments remain under executive control, crimes under international law have not yet been incorporated into national law, and the death penalty remains available.

explore_lenses.label: How did the case reach a death sentence now?
explore_lenses.title: It traces back to the 2011 Daraa crackdown
explore_lenses.summary: The proceedings focus on the repression of early protests in Daraa, a pivotal episode in the uprising that became Syria's war. Najib's presence in custody allowed an in-person trial, while Assad, Maher Assad, and other former officials were prosecuted as fugitives.

claims.text: Atef Najib, then head of the Political Security Branch in Daraa, was accused in connection with the violent suppression of early 2011 protests; the detention and torture of teenagers there helped spark the broader uprising.
The Fourth Criminal Court opened Najib's case on April 26, 2026, and recorded Assad, Maher Assad, and other named defendants as absent; the court proceeded under Syria's in-absentia procedures.

According to Reuters reporting, the judgment convicted Assad of premeditated intentional murder, including of children, torture, arbitrary arrest, and crimes against humanity; Maher received the same sentence.

The Syrian Network for Human Rights said before the verdict that the legal durability of the case would depend on the court clearly explaining its legal basis, including how it addressed non-retroactivity and the procedural interests of absent defendants.

story_report.summary: A Damascus criminal court sentenced former Syrian president Bashar al-Assad and his brother Maher to death in absentia after convicting them of crimes including crimes against humanity, war crimes, premeditated murder, torture and arbitrary arrest. Their cousin Atef Najib was tried in person in proceedings tied to the violent suppression of protests in Daraa at the start of Syria’s civil war, a conflict estimated to have killed about half a million people. Assad and Maher remain in Russia, leaving enforcement dependent on developments beyond the court’s immediate control.

sections.heading: Daraa case traces uprising origins
sections.body: The case centered on Najib’s role as head of the Political Security Branch in Daraa, where he was accused in connection with the crackdown on early 2011 demonstrations. The detention and torture of teenagers in the city helped trigger the wider uprising. The Fourth Criminal Court opened Najib’s case on April 26, 2026, recording Assad, Maher Assad and other defendants as absent and proceeding under Syrian in-absentia procedures. Trial monitors described the proceedings as the first public national criminal case against a senior Assad-era security figure.

sections.heading: Rights groups question legal safeguards
sections.body: Amnesty International has identified continuing concerns over Syria’s accountability framework, saying judicial appointments remain under executive control, crimes under international law have not been incorporated into national law, and the death penalty remains available. The Syrian Network for Human Rights said before the verdict that the case’s durability would depend on a clear legal explanation, including treatment of non-retroactivity and the procedural interests of defendants tried in absentia. The full written judgment and a complete public account of the evidence and legal reasoning were not located in the consulted sources.

sections.heading: Russian refuge limits sentence enforcement
sections.body: Assad fled to Moscow after his government collapsed in December 2024, and Maher Assad also fled to Russia. Anwar al-Bunni of the Syrian Centre for Legal Studies and Research told Reuters that death sentences could reduce the chance of foreign surrender, as some states may decline to extradite people who could face execution. SNHR executive director Fadel Abdulghany said Russian protection left no realistic near-term prospect of arrest or extradition, though he argued that a well-grounded ruling could provide an official record for future accountability efforts.

unresolved.text: It remains unclear how the court addressed evidentiary issues, command responsibility, notification and defense rights, because publicly available reporting does not establish those matters.
Russia’s position on any request to transfer Assad or Maher Assad, the post-verdict remedies available to absent defendants, and any timetable for enforcing the sentences remain unresolved.

stories.title: Ukrainian Drone Strike on Russian Oil Refinery Claims 13 Lives
stories.summary: A Ukrainian drone strike on the Taneco oil refinery in Nizhnekamsk, Russia, has resulted in the deaths of at least 13 people and injuries to 78 others. This attack, which occurred deep inside Russian territory, is reported to be one of the deadliest since the onset of the war. The strike is part of Ukraine's ongoing campaign to target critical infrastructure far from the frontline.

event_overview.title: About Russia-Ukraine War
event_overview.subject: Russia-Ukraine War
event_overview.summary: The Russia-Ukraine War is an ongoing armed conflict between Ukraine and the Russian Federation, rooted in fighting that began in eastern Ukraine in 2014 and greatly escalated with Russia’s full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022. It has involved conventional ground operations as well as long-range missile and drone attacks, and has produced a major humanitarian and displacement crisis.

facts.label: Origins and escalation
facts.value: Conflict-related humanitarian operations in eastern Ukraine expanded in 2014; Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022 transformed the conflict into a nationwide emergency.

facts.label: Main parties and geography
facts.value: The war principally involves Ukraine and the Russian Federation, with military operations taking place in Ukraine and attacks increasingly affecting areas beyond the immediate front line.

facts.label: International legal position
facts.value: On March 2, 2022, the UN General Assembly deplored Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, demanded that Russia end its use of force and withdraw its forces, and reaffirmed Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders.

facts.label: International Court of Justice proceedin
facts.value: In provisional measures issued on March 16, 2022 in Ukraine v. Russian Federation, the International Court of Justice ordered Russia to suspend military operations begun on February 24, 2022, while stating that the order did not decide the case’s merits.

facts.label: Humanitarian impact
facts.value: The war has driven large-scale displacement, damaged civilian infrastructure and left millions of people in need of assistance; UNHCR describes it as an ongoing full-scale war and humanitarian emergency.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline focuses on specified late-July and early-August 2026 security developments, including cross-border drone or missile incidents and strikes; it does not aim to provide a complete account of the war’s military, diplomatic, legal, or humanitarian history.

explore_lenses.label: Why was the Taneco refinery a significant target?
explore_lenses.title: A major refining and fuel-production complex
explore_lenses.summary: Taneco is a large Tatneft refining and petrochemical complex in Nizhnekamsk, making it relevant to Ukraine's stated strategy of placing economic and military-industrial pressure on Russia. Its importance does not by itself establish the strike's actual production impact.

claims.text: Tatneft said in 2021 that Taneco had 21 operating technological units, targeted crude-processing volumes above 15 million tonnes annually, and a 99% refining depth.

Tatneft and Russia's Energy Ministry described planned Taneco investments as supporting products including Euro-5 gasoline and Arctic diesel fuel, and the company said the project contributed to Russia's energy security.
Ukraine's stated rationale is to reduce the military potential of the Russian state; the reported refinery strike fits that stated objective.

story_report.summary: A Ukrainian drone strike hit the Taneco oil refinery in Nizhnekamsk, about 750 miles from Ukraine’s border, killing at least 13 people and injuring 78, according to reported official figures. The attack, described as one of the deadliest of the war, brought the consequences of Ukraine’s long-range campaign deep into Russian territory. Tatarstan’s leader declared a day of mourning, while Russian prosecutors opened a criminal case alleging terrorism.

sections.heading: Taneco Refinery’s Reported Capacity
sections.body: Taneco is a major Tatneft refining project. In a 2021 company statement, Tatneft said the site had 21 operating technological units, sought annual crude-processing volumes above 15 million tonnes and had achieved a 99% refining depth. Tatneft and Russia’s Energy Ministry said planned investment supported products including Euro-5 gasoline and Arctic diesel, while the company characterized the project as contributing to Russia’s energy security.

sections.heading: Ukraine Frames Long-Range Campaign
sections.body: Ukraine has said its objective is to reduce the Russian state’s military potential, a rationale into which the reported refinery strike fits. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said pressure on the Kremlin and its war machine would continue, framing the campaign as a response to Russian strikes on Ukrainian towns and cities. A member of a Ukrainian strike-drone brigade forecast continued operations and cascading pressure on Russian-held Crimea, but that prediction is not an independently established outcome.

unresolved.text: Tatneft’s 2021 capacity figures do not independently establish Taneco’s production level immediately before or after the strike.
The consulted reporting identified no confirmed diplomatic initiative, retaliatory operation or verified timetable for refinery repairs.

Additionally, reports indicate that overnight attacks across Ukraine have left at least nine people dead and many more wounded.

explore_lenses.label: What changed in the August 11 strikes?
explore_lenses.title: A broad overnight attack hit several regions
explore_lenses.summary: The reported attack combined multiple weapon types and affected Zaporizhzhia, Kyiv and Dnipropetrovsk. The immediate human toll is reported by Ukrainian regional authorities; the Russian Defence Ministry said it targeted military-industrial and transport-logistics sites.

claims.text: Zaporizhzhia regional administration head Ivan Fedorov said six people were killed and 19 injured after a large attack involving missiles and guided aerial bombs.
Authorities in Dnipropetrovsk reported three deaths and five injuries across five districts, while Kyiv authorities reported a ballistic-missile alert and a warehouse fire that injured one person.

stories.title: Ebola Outbreak in Congo Claims Over 2,000 Lives, Marked as Fastest Growing on Record
stories.summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo reports that at least 2,000 people have died in its ongoing Ebola outbreak, which is now recognized as the fastest growing on record. As of the latest updates, there have been 4,381 confirmed cases across five provinces. The outbreak reportedly began months before it was officially declared in May, complicating response efforts due to factors such as rebel conflict and infrastructure challenges.

event_overview.title: About Congo Ebola Outbreak
event_overview.subject: Congo Ebola Outbreak
event_overview.summary: This is the 2026 Ebola disease outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with epidemiologically linked cases reported in neighboring Uganda. The outbreak was declared in May 2026 and has expanded from its initial focus in northeastern DRC amid insecurity, population movement, and constraints on surveillance, isolation, and care.

facts.label: Start and official declaration
facts.value: DRC health authorities declared the country’s 17th recorded Ebola outbreak on May 15, 2026, after the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease in samples associated with illness clusters in Ituri Province.

facts.label: Virus involved
facts.value: The event involves Bundibugyo virus disease, rather than the Zaire ebolavirus responsible for DRC’s 2018–2020 outbreak. WHO states that no approved vaccine or specific treatment existed for this virus as the 2026 outbreak began, although candidate countermeasures were being studied.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: Transmission began in Ituri Province, including Mongbwalu, Rwampara and Bunia health zones, and later spread to other DRC provinces. Uganda’s cases were linked to transmission originating in DRC, making this a cross-border regional outbreak rather than an outbreak confined to one locality.

facts.label: International health status
facts.value: On May 17, 2026, the WHO Director-General determined that the epidemic in DRC and Uganda constituted a Public Health Emergency of International Concern under the International Health Regulations, while stating that it did not meet the separate criteria for a pandemic emergency.

facts.label: Response approach
facts.value: The response is led by the national health authorities with WHO and partner support, emphasizing rapid detection and laboratory confirmation, isolation and clinical care, contact tracing, infection prevention, safe burials, community engagement, and cross-border preparedness.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows major reported developments in the 2026 DRC outbreak—such as reported tolls, geographic or regional status, treatment capacity, and workforce issues—rather than providing a complete case ledger, every official situation report, or the full history of Ebola in Central Africa.

explore_lenses.title: Remote communities and frontline staff face the greatest burden
explore_lenses.summary: The outbreak is concentrated in eastern DRC, where access to timely diagnosis and isolation is constrained by conflict, displacement, poor transport and disruptions to the health workforce. Ebola spreads through direct contact with infectious body fluids, making household care and delayed presentation especially consequential.

claims.text: CDC reported that the early DRC clusters included health care workers and that, as of June 2, cases were primarily among adults ages 18–49; the available data then showed an approximately even female-male distribution.

The AP reported that unpaid-worker strikes, rebel conflict, poor roads, limited protective gear and displacement are impeding outreach to affected localities; some residents are also avoiding health centers because they fear infection.

Bundibugyo virus is expected to spread through direct contact with the body fluids of infected people or people who have died; patients are thought to be most infectious late in illness and after death.

explore_lenses.label: What could determine whether cases keep accelerating?
explore_lenses.title: Case isolation and finding untracked transmission are pivotal
explore_lenses.summary: CDC modeling found sharply different projected outcomes depending on how many symptomatic patients are detected and isolated. But those are scenario projections, not a prediction that a particular total will occur, and the model was calibrated to data from May rather than the August 11 case count.

claims.text: CDC's model projected that, under a scenario with only 20% of symptomatic patients isolated and no other interventions, there was a 65% chance of exceeding 20,000 cases within three months; with 70% isolation, it projected a one-in-20 chance of reaching 10,000 or more cases within three months.

The model's assumptions included a possible spillover event in mid-to-late February and simulated intervention intensity as the share of symptomatic patients successfully isolated; it does not establish that those assumptions precisely describe current transmission.
Health authorities said 60%–70% of newly recorded cases were outside monitored contacts, a sign that many transmission chains were not yet being captured by contact tracing.
CDC assessed the outbreak's scope as likely larger than the available data show because it is occurring amid limited health infrastructure, armed conflict, displacement and cross-border movement.

story_report.summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported at least 2,000 deaths and 4,381 confirmed Ebola cases across five provinces. The rising toll is testing an already difficult response: unpaid-worker strikes, rebel conflict, poor roads, limited protective equipment and displacement have impeded outreach, while some residents have avoided health centers because they fear infection. Health authorities also say many newly recorded cases are not among monitored contacts, complicating efforts to trace transmission chains.

sections.heading: Origins and Viral Identification
sections.body: WHO officials said genetic sequencing indicates transmission began in February 2026, roughly three months before the May 15 outbreak declaration. Early infections were reportedly attributed to malaria or typhoid. Laboratory analysis confirmed Bundibugyo virus, and CDC said the sequencing was consistent with a new zoonotic spillover event from an unknown host; the virus is expected to spread through direct contact with infected people’s body fluids, including after death.

sections.heading: Barriers to Case Detection
sections.body: Health authorities said 60% to 70% of newly recorded cases were outside monitored contacts, indicating that contact tracing was not capturing many transmission chains. CDC’s early June snapshot found cases primarily among adults ages 18 to 49, with an approximately even female-male distribution, and included health care workers among early clusters. Those demographic findings reflect an early point in the outbreak rather than a current profile.

sections.heading: Care and Response Projections
sections.body: CDC said no vaccine or medication for Bundibugyo virus disease had been approved, leaving supportive care as the available treatment. In a model assuming only 20% of symptomatic patients were isolated and no other interventions, CDC projected a 65% chance of more than 20,000 cases within three months. Under a 70% isolation scenario, the model projected a one-in-20 chance of at least 10,000 cases, though the projections depend on assumptions that may not precisely reflect current transmission.

unresolved.text: The initial spillover source remains unknown, and the estimated February start is based on genomic and epidemiological reconstruction rather than direct observation of the first infection.
The number of unreported infections and deaths remains unresolved, particularly in areas affected by weak health access, conflict, displacement and limits on testing and care.

event_overview.title: About Iran Threats
event_overview.subject: Iran Threats
event_overview.summary: This event concerns reported protective travel measures taken during President Donald Trump’s departure from the NATO summit in Ankara, Türkiye, on July 8, 2026. U.S. officials told news outlets that intelligence indicated a credible threat involving Iran and Iran-aligned proxy groups, leading to the reported use of a different presidential aircraft; the specific threat details have not been publicly documented by the U.S. government.

facts.label: Date and location
facts.value: The reported aircraft change occurred as Trump departed Ankara, Türkiye, after the July 7-8, 2026 NATO summit.

facts.label: Summit context
facts.value: Türkiye hosted the 2026 NATO summit at the Beştepe Presidential Compound in Ankara; NATO describes summits as meetings of Allied heads of state and government that provide strategic direction for the Alliance.

facts.label: Reported protective measure
facts.value: CBS News reported, citing U.S. officials, that Trump departed on the older Air Force One aircraft rather than the newer Qatar-donated plane after intelligence identified a credible threat to the president from Iran and allied proxy groups.

facts.label: Nature of the allegation
facts.value: The reporting characterized the intelligence as involving a possible missile attack on the president’s aircraft. This was an account attributed to unnamed officials, rather than a publicly released U.S. intelligence finding or criminal case.

facts.label: Protection responsibility
facts.value: The U.S. Secret Service’s protective mission includes ensuring the safety of the president, alongside other protected officials, visiting heads of state, and designated events.

story_report.summary: President Donald Trump was discreetly moved from Air Force One to another U.S. government aircraft after the NATO summit in Ankara, according to reports citing officials. The transfer, carried out through a catering truck, followed intelligence indicating an alleged Iranian and proxy missile plot against the aircraft carrying him. The public departure aboard the older presidential jet functioned as a decoy, while the press pool and some staff remained on that plane as Trump traveled separately. Both aircraft later reached Britain minutes apart.

sections.heading: Trump’s Ankara Departure Operation
sections.body: NATO says its Ankara summit was held July 7-8, 2026, placing the reported operation at the meeting’s conclusion. CBS News reported that Trump visibly boarded the older Air Force One before being taken by catering truck to another U.S. government aircraft. The Guardian, citing the Washington Post and New York Times, identified the alternate plane as a C-32A and reported that it and the decoy aircraft landed in Britain only minutes apart.

sections.heading: Iran Threat Reports and Response
sections.body: CBS reported that U.S. intelligence had detected what it described as a credible plan by Iran and allied proxies to fire a missile at Trump’s aircraft. Before departing, Trump publicly said he would fly the older plane “for old time’s sake,” while CBS separately reported that the Secret Service had recommended the older jet for security reasons. White House communications director Steven Cheung did not directly address the switch, saying instead that the Qatari-donated aircraft had high-level security protocols and that the administration used every available tool against threats to the president.

explore_lenses.label: Does evidence support spacing out vaccines?
explore_lenses.title: Pediatric guidance supports on-time, simultaneous vaccination
explore_lenses.summary: The American Academy of Pediatrics says routine vaccines given at the same visit are safe and effective and that delaying them extends the period in which a child is unprotected. The administration frames the policy as increasing parental flexibility, but the supplied reporting does not establish new clinical evidence supporting an alternative timetable.

claims.text: AAP's Red Book says simultaneous administration of most vaccines on the recommended schedule is safe and effective; immune responses and adverse-event rates are generally similar to those when the vaccines are given at separate visits.

AAP says there is no medical reason to delay or space routine childhood immunizations, and that alternative schedules have not been studied for safety or effectiveness; it says delay increases the time children remain at risk of vaccine-preventable disease.
A White House spokesperson told AP that separate MMR vaccines would give parents more options on timing and frequency and said this would increase vaccination rates for all three diseases.

story_report.summary: President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Aug. 10, 2026, seeking to limit childhood vaccinations to 11 immunizations and promote giving shots at separate visits. The order also calls for federal officials to develop a plan for separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines, which are not currently available in the United States. Its immediate effect is uncertain, however: the CDC says a court order has stayed an earlier schedule revision and identifies its July 2025 schedule as current.

sections.heading: Current CDC Schedule Remains in Place
sections.body: The CDC’s current childhood schedule includes routine recommendations beyond the 11 diseases in the earlier proposal, including hepatitis B, rotavirus, influenza, hepatitis A and meningococcal disease, with some guidance varying by age or risk. Protection against several illnesses begins in infancy: hepatitis B is recommended at birth, while rotavirus, DTaP, Hib and pneumococcal vaccines begin at about 2 months. The schedule also includes special recommendations for children with particular health risks.

sections.heading: Pediatricians Challenge Spaced Vaccination Plan
sections.body: The American Academy of Pediatrics says giving most recommended vaccines at the same visit is safe and effective, with immune responses and adverse-event rates generally similar to those seen when shots are separated. The group says there is no medical reason to delay routine immunizations, that alternative schedules have not been studied for safety or effectiveness, and that delays leave children at risk longer. A White House spokesperson, by contrast, told AP that separate MMR products would give parents more control over timing and frequency and could raise vaccination rates for all three diseases.

sections.heading: Vaccination Coverage Creates Implementation Stakes
sections.body: CDC says routine childhood vaccination coverage has not recovered in some groups affected by pandemic-era declines, including young children living in poverty or rural areas, kindergartners and Medicaid-eligible adolescents. AAP infectious-disease specialists warn that policies encouraging parents to postpone vaccination could increase illnesses that have become rare in the United States. The eventual effects on vaccine uptake, completion of multi-dose series and disease incidence cannot yet be measured and will depend on implementation and decisions by families and clinicians.

unresolved.text: It remains unresolved whether, when and through which regulatory or advisory process the executive order will result in a legally operative revised childhood schedule or separate MMR vaccines.
No published estimate in the available evidence quantifies how many additional appointments a spaced schedule would require or which families would be least able to complete it.

event_overview.title: About Iran Relations
event_overview.subject: Iran Relations
event_overview.summary: Iran relations in this timeline concern the long-running, largely adversarial relationship between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran, shaped by the absence of formal diplomatic ties, sanctions, nuclear-policy disputes, and security issues in the Persian Gulf. The immediate context also includes the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway between Iran and Oman whose security affects international energy shipments.

facts.label: Diplomatic status
facts.value: The United States severed diplomatic relations with Iran on April 7, 1980; Switzerland serves as the protecting power for U.S. interests in Iran.

facts.label: Nuclear diplomacy framework
facts.value: Iran, China, France, Germany, Russia, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the European Union concluded the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) on July 14, 2015. The UN Security Council unanimously endorsed it through Resolution 2231 on July 20, 2015.

facts.label: International nuclear verification
facts.value: Iran's safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), connected to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, entered into force on May 15, 1974; the IAEA is the international body responsible for applying those safeguards.

facts.label: U.S. economic measures
facts.value: U.S. Iran sanctions are administered and enforced by the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control under multiple statutes, executive orders, regulations, and, where applicable, UN Security Council measures.

facts.label: Strait of Hormuz
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz lies between Iran and Oman and connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea, making it a major oil-transit chokepoint.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers specific developments from August 2 through August 11, 2026 involving reported U.S.-Iran diplomacy, military pressure, and Strait of Hormuz access; it does not attempt to cover the full history of U.S.-Iran relations, all nuclear negotiations, sanctions actions, or regional security events.

explore_lenses.label: What happens next procedurally?
explore_lenses.title: Routes may advance before a full deal
explore_lenses.summary: The clearest near-term process is work through intermediaries on limited shipping arrangements, not a confirmed full reopening. That track is occurring alongside incompatible public claims over control of the strait and conditions for ending restrictions.

claims.text: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said an agreement with Oman on defining new shipping routes was in its final stages, while stressing that this would not itself mean the Strait of Hormuz had reopened.
Araghchi said other conditions had been conveyed to the U.S. through intermediaries, indicating that indirect diplomacy remains the reported channel.

The White House said in July that Trump viewed a deal as possible but asserted U.S. control of the strait and said Iran could still disrupt transit with mines; these are administration claims rather than a jointly accepted account.

Euronews reported that Trump described Washington as only semi-negotiating and willing to allow economic pressure on Iran to continue rather than immediately resume a military campaign; this suggests a slower negotiating approach, not a settled procedure or deadline.

points: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said an agreement with Oman on defining new shipping routes was in its final stages, while stressing that this would not itself mean the Strait of Hormuz had reopened.
Araghchi said other conditions had been conveyed to the U.S. through intermediaries, indicating that indirect diplomacy remains the reported channel.

The White House said in July that Trump viewed a deal as possible but asserted U.S. control of the strait and said Iran could still disrupt transit with mines; these are administration claims rather than a jointly accepted account.

Euronews reported that Trump described Washington as only semi-negotiating and willing to allow economic pressure on Iran to continue rather than immediately resume a military campaign; this suggests a slower negotiating approach, not a settled procedure or deadline.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War is the 2026 armed conflict involving the United States, Iran and Israel, centered on attacks, counterattacks and threats affecting Iran, neighboring states and maritime traffic in and around the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz. U.S. officials said combat operations began on February 28, 2026, citing self-defense, protection of regional forces and allies, and freedom of maritime commerce; the United Nations has called for de-escalation, protection of civilians and compliance with international law.

facts.label: Start and parties
facts.value: The conflict’s current phase began on February 28, 2026. The United States notified the UN that it had commenced combat operations against Iran in cooperation with Israel; the UN Secretary-General also described subsequent Iranian attacks affecting Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Geographic focus
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz—between Iran and Oman, linking the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea—is a central theater because its security directly affects regional shipping and energy exports.

facts.label: Maritime and energy stakes
facts.value: Disruption to shipping through Hormuz has been a major international consequence: EIA reported that military action and the resulting de facto closure sharply reduced oil flows and contributed to large price increases in early 2026.

facts.label: Diplomatic and legal framework
facts.value: The UN has urged an immediate cessation of hostilities and stated that all parties must uphold the UN Charter, protect civilians under international humanitarian law and preserve nuclear safety. In the United States, the War Powers Resolution requires presidential consultation with Congress where possible and a written report within 48 hours when U.S. forces are introduced into hostilities without a declaration of wa

facts.label: Broader policy context
facts.value: The conflict occurs alongside longstanding international concern over Iran’s nuclear programme. UN Security Council Resolution 2231, adopted in 2015 to endorse the JCPOA, remains part of that background; the UN says earlier Iran-related Security Council measures were re-applied on September 27, 2025.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline focuses on late-July 2026 escalation, congressional war-powers action, Houthi-linked regional attacks, oil-market effects and ceasefire diplomacy; it does not attempt to document the conflict’s full military, humanitarian, diplomatic or legal history.

event_overview.title: About Russia-Ukraine War
event_overview.subject: Russia-Ukraine War
event_overview.summary: The Russia-Ukraine War is an ongoing armed conflict between Ukraine and the Russian Federation, rooted in fighting that began in eastern Ukraine in 2014 and greatly escalated with Russia’s full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022. It has involved conventional ground operations as well as long-range missile and drone attacks, and has produced a major humanitarian and displacement crisis.

facts.label: Origins and escalation
facts.value: Conflict-related humanitarian operations in eastern Ukraine expanded in 2014; Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022 transformed the conflict into a nationwide emergency.

facts.label: Main parties and geography
facts.value: The war principally involves Ukraine and the Russian Federation, with military operations taking place in Ukraine and attacks increasingly affecting areas beyond the immediate front line.

facts.label: International legal position
facts.value: On March 2, 2022, the UN General Assembly deplored Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, demanded that Russia end its use of force and withdraw its forces, and reaffirmed Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders.

facts.label: International Court of Justice proceedin
facts.value: In provisional measures issued on March 16, 2022 in Ukraine v. Russian Federation, the International Court of Justice ordered Russia to suspend military operations begun on February 24, 2022, while stating that the order did not decide the case’s merits.

facts.label: Humanitarian impact
facts.value: The war has driven large-scale displacement, damaged civilian infrastructure and left millions of people in need of assistance; UNHCR describes it as an ongoing full-scale war and humanitarian emergency.

story_report.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel has rejected Donald Trump’s 15-point Gaza roadmap, insisting that Israeli forces will not withdraw until Hamas is genuinely and fully disarmed. The stance creates an immediate dispute over the sequence of withdrawal and weapons decommissioning, although discussions between Israel and the United States were continuing. The proposal’s broader transition arrangements, including international verification of disarmament, therefore remain unsettled.

sections.heading: Roadmap Sets Phased Gaza Transition
sections.body: A May report by the Board of Peace outlined a phased process for internationally verified weapons decommissioning, paired with steps by Israel and other parties. It envisaged an Israeli military withdrawal to Gaza’s perimeter as verified progress was made. The roadmap assigned civilian administration and security to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, while requiring Hamas and other armed factions to end their military, policing and administrative roles.

sections.heading: Hamas and Israel Differ on Terms
sections.body: Netanyahu’s position is that Israel cannot withdraw while Hamas retains weapons. Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim said the group remained committed to the roadmap and expected mediators and the United States to press Israel to follow it. AP reported that Hamas has expressed willingness to hand civilian governance to a committee, but has sought an interim administration and police force before a technocratic handover and has resisted immediately surrendering its arsenal.

sections.heading: Disarmament Stalemate Risks Renewed Fighting
sections.body: The plan proposes an International Stabilisation Force to buffer Gaza, protect humanitarian operations and support weapons custody, with reconstruction beginning in certified decommissioned areas under NCAG authority. Board of Peace envoy Nickolay Mladenov said the ceasefire and wider transition hinge on disarmament, warning that failure to resolve the issue could leave Gaza vulnerable to renewed large-scale fighting and stalled reconstruction.

unresolved.text: The full July 31 version of the proposed roadmap and Israel’s specific written objections were not publicly available in the reviewed sources.
It remains unclear who would verify disarmament, when and where Israeli withdrawals would occur, and on what terms an international stabilization force would deploy.
The sources do not establish whether Hamas accepts complete independently verified disarmament or whether Israel would accept an amended roadmap.

event_overview.title: About Typhoon Dolphin
event_overview.subject: Typhoon Dolphin
event_overview.summary: Typhoon Dolphin was the 13th named tropical cyclone of the 2026 western North Pacific season, forming in late July and later tracking westward across the region. It affected Japan’s Okinawa area before making landfall in Zhejiang province on China’s east coast; by August 10 it had weakened to a tropical storm inland.

facts.label: Formation and designation
facts.value: China’s National Meteorological Center designated Dolphin as 2026’s No. 13 typhoon; official reporting said it formed over the northwestern Pacific on July 27, 2026.

facts.label: China landfall and weakening
facts.value: Dolphin made landfall near Taizhou, Zhejiang, on the evening of August 9 with reported winds of 151 kph; on August 10, China’s National Meteorological Center listed it as a tropical storm over Dexing, Jiangxi, and forecast further weakening.

facts.label: Naming system
facts.value: “Dolphin” is a name contributed by Hong Kong, China, under the ESCAP/WMO Typhoon Committee naming list; it refers to the Chinese white dolphin and a Hong Kong mascot.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the August 8-10 Japan-to-China impact period and preparedness or disruption measures, not Dolphin’s full late-July development, its complete inland dissipation, or all effects elsewhere in the region.

story_report.summary: Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in eastern China at Taizhou, Zhejiang, with winds of about 151 km/h, bringing heavy rain, strong winds and warnings of severe flooding and landslides. Contemporaneous reports said more than one million people were evacuated as authorities moved residents from vulnerable areas. The storm also disrupted travel, with Shanghai airport cancellations reported in the hundreds and more than 1,300 flights later cited across the city’s two airports.

sections.heading: Transport and Services Face Disruption
sections.body: Shanghai’s two airports canceled more than 1,300 flights, while authorities in Zhejiang suspended ferries and cruises. Ningbo closed schools and halted water-related activities before landfall, and tourist destinations across Zhejiang shut or suspended operations. The consulted sources did not give a confirmed timetable for restoring flights, ferry services, schools or tourism operations.

sections.heading: Dolphin Weakens on Inland Track
sections.body: At 19:00 on August 10, China’s National Meteorological Center listed Dolphin in Dexing, Jiangxi province, with sustained winds of 20 metres per second, or about 72 km/h. The agency forecast that the storm would continue northwest or west-northwest at roughly 15-20 km/h, gradually weaken and eventually dissipate.

sections.heading: Local Evacuations Preceded Landfall
sections.body: Before landfall, authorities reported relocating more than 300,000 people, including about 390,000 evacuees in Taizhou and more than 30,000 people from higher-risk parts of Shanghai. The reported figures were compiled at different stages and locations, meaning they are not directly comparable. Flooding was reported in parts of eastern China, where Yueqing authorities searched flooded homes and cleared storm debris.

event_overview.title: About Crime Extradition
event_overview.subject: Crime Extradition
event_overview.summary: This event concerns the transfer of Irish national Daniel Kinahan from the United Arab Emirates to Ireland under the two countries’ extradition framework, so that he can face criminal proceedings in Ireland. Reporting on the transfer said he was expected to appear before Ireland’s Special Criminal Court on an allegation of directing an organized crime group; the allegation remains to be determined through the Irish judicial process.

facts.label: Extradition framework
facts.value: Ireland and the UAE concluded their bilateral extradition treaty in Abu Dhabi on October 21, 2024. Ireland’s Extradition (United Arab Emirates) Order 2025 brought the UAE within Part II of Ireland’s Extradition Act 1965 from May 18, 2025.

facts.label: Legal scope
facts.value: Under the treaty, either state may seek a person for prosecution, trial, or execution of a sentence. For a prosecution request, the conduct must be punishable in both states by at least one year of imprisonment.

facts.label: Responsible authorities
facts.value: The treaty names Ireland’s Minister for Justice, or departmental officials exercising the minister’s functions, as Ireland’s central authority; the UAE Ministry of Justice is the UAE central authority.

facts.label: Broader enforcement context
facts.value: In April 2022, the U.S. Treasury Department designated the Kinahan Organized Crime Group and Daniel Kinahan under its transnational-crime sanctions authority; sanctions are an administrative measure and separate from the Irish criminal case.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the reported August 9–10, 2026 transfer and initial Irish charging stage, not the full history of the Kinahan group, the UAE court process, or the eventual outcome of any Irish prosecution.

The directing-a-criminal-organisation offence can apply to conduct outside Ireland and carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment on conviction on indictment.

explore_lenses.title: The charge moves into court process
explore_lenses.summary: The immediate issue is the Irish criminal process—custody or bail, disclosure, plea, and eventual trial—not further extradition proceedings. Organised-crime cases are generally tried in Ireland's Special Criminal Court, a three-judge court without a jury.

claims.text: The Courts Service says cases involving organised-crime offences are automatically brought before the Special Criminal Court for trial; it sits with three judges and no jury.
A Special Criminal Court conviction or sentence can be appealed to the Court of Appeal.

The prosecution must establish the statutory elements of directing the organisation; the law permits the court to consider, alongside other relevant evidence, a pattern of behaviour consistent with directing it and whether the accused benefited from it.

sections.heading: Ireland-UAE extradition cooperation
sections.body: Ireland and the United Arab Emirates brought extradition and mutual-legal-assistance treaties into force on 18 May 2025 after completing their respective legal procedures. The Justice Department said the agreements were intended to structure and simplify cooperation while retaining safeguards related to human rights, the death penalty and mistreatment. Sean McGovern’s transfer to Ireland in May 2025 was reported as the first extradition from the UAE to Ireland.

sections.heading: Directing organization charge process
sections.body: RTÉ reported that investigators submitted a file to the Director of Public Prosecutions, who directed that Kinahan be charged; Gardaí subsequently obtained a High Court arrest warrant and sent it to UAE authorities. The offence can cover conduct outside Ireland and carries a maximum life sentence on conviction on indictment. Prosecutors must prove its statutory elements; the law allows a court to consider a relevant pattern of behaviour and whether an accused benefited from the organization, alongside other evidence.

sections.heading: Special Criminal Court proceedings
sections.body: The Courts Service says organized-crime offences are automatically brought before the Special Criminal Court, which hears cases without a jury and with three judges. Any conviction or sentence can be appealed to the Court of Appeal. Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan said Kinahan’s April 2026 arrest followed Ireland’s extradition request and credited Garda investigators, prosecutors, Irish government departments and UAE counterparts.

explore_lenses.title: It describes a treatable cancer subtype, not a prognosis
explore_lenses.summary: The original announcement said the cancer appeared hormone-sensitive. In metastatic prostate cancer, that generally means cancer growth can still be suppressed by reducing or blocking androgens, but it does not establish how long treatment will work for an individual patient.

claims.text: Biden’s office said in May 2025 that the cancer appeared hormone-sensitive, which it said allowed for effective management.

The National Cancer Institute says metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer is commonly treated with androgen-deprivation therapy combined with another hormone therapy, and in some cases chemotherapy.

The National Cancer Institute says clinicians cannot predict how long hormone therapy will suppress cancer growth for any individual patient; PSA testing is used to monitor whether the disease may be growing again or becoming resistant.

explore_lenses.label: Why does a provincial emergency matter?
explore_lenses.title: It expands coordination and support capacity
explore_lenses.summary: The declaration is not itself a firefighting tactic; it is a province-wide mechanism for coordinating a fast-moving emergency and supporting displaced residents. Federal assistance has already been directed toward shelter and accommodations.

claims.text: Premier David Eby declared a provincial state of emergency on August 8 after the Bald Range fire spread rapidly and evacuation orders expanded around Summerland and Peachland.

Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski said she approved British Columbia's request for federal assistance to provide shelter and accommodations for evacuees, with Public Safety Canada's Government Operations Centre coordinating the federal response.
Officials had reported significant structure loss, but the extent could not yet be assessed because affected areas remained active fire zones.

explore_lenses.label: How did the fire danger build so quickly?
explore_lenses.title: Drought, heat and wind created volatile conditions
explore_lenses.summary: The immediate crisis followed a period of moisture deficit and unusually dry fuels in parts of southern British Columbia. The Bald Range fire's early growth illustrates how wind and dry vegetation can rapidly turn an ignition into a community-threatening event.

claims.text: BC Wildfire Service's June seasonal outlook identified long-term precipitation deficits and above-average drought in the Okanagan, and said low snowpack, a dry spring and warm conditions were increasing wildfire risk.
The agency's outlook forecast that fire activity would peak in July and August, while emphasizing that later-season conditions would still depend on rainfall.

The Bald Range wildfire was first reported on August 7 and grew to more than 100 square kilometres within hours as it moved roughly 15 kilometres toward Okanagan Lake, according to reporting citing BC Wildfire Service information.

Wildfire expert Mike Flannigan attributed the rapid spread to extreme dryness and said higher-intensity fires are increasingly difficult to manage; this is an expert assessment rather than an official finding on the ignition or full cause of this specific fire.

story_report.summary: British Columbia has declared a provincial state of emergency as more than 100 wildfires burn, with nearly half listed as out of control. About 22,000 people have been evacuated, while another 10,000 have been told to prepare to leave on short notice. The emergency declaration followed the rapid spread of the Bald Range fire and expanding evacuation orders around Summerland and Peachland, prompting federal support for evacuee shelter and accommodations.

sections.heading: Bald Range Fire Drives Evacuations
sections.body: The Bald Range wildfire was first reported on August 7 and grew to more than 100 square kilometres within hours, moving roughly 15 kilometres toward Okanagan Lake, according to reporting citing BC Wildfire Service information. Officials reported significant structure loss, though they could not assess the full extent while affected areas remained active fire zones. Response efforts included 10 standard helicopters and one helicopter equipped for night operations.

sections.heading: Drought Conditions Raised Wildfire Risk
sections.body: BC Wildfire Service’s June outlook identified long-term precipitation deficits and above-average drought in the Okanagan. It said low snowpack, a dry spring and warm conditions were increasing wildfire risk, and forecast peak fire activity in July and August, while noting that later-season conditions would depend on rainfall. Wildfire expert Mike Flannigan said extreme dryness helped explain rapid spread and that higher-intensity fires are increasingly difficult to manage; his assessment was not an official finding on the cause of the Bald Range fire.

sections.heading: Thunderstorms Could Complicate Fire Response
sections.body: BC Wildfire Service director of provincial operations Cliff Chapman said thunderstorms forecast for the coming week could worsen conditions by creating lightning-caused ignitions. The agency had also said rainfall sufficient to ease persistent drought in regions including the Okanagan was unlikely during the summer, while cautioning that long-range forecasts can change. Federal authorities are coordinating assistance through Public Safety Canada’s Government Operations Centre after approving British Columbia’s request for evacuee shelter and accommodations.

event_overview.title: About Typhoon Dolphin
event_overview.subject: Typhoon Dolphin
event_overview.summary: Typhoon Dolphin was the 13th named tropical cyclone of the 2026 western North Pacific season, forming in late July and later tracking westward across the region. It affected Japan’s Okinawa area before making landfall in Zhejiang province on China’s east coast; by August 10 it had weakened to a tropical storm inland.

facts.label: Formation and designation
facts.value: China’s National Meteorological Center designated Dolphin as 2026’s No. 13 typhoon; official reporting said it formed over the northwestern Pacific on July 27, 2026.

facts.label: China landfall and weakening
facts.value: Dolphin made landfall near Taizhou, Zhejiang, on the evening of August 9 with reported winds of 151 kph; on August 10, China’s National Meteorological Center listed it as a tropical storm over Dexing, Jiangxi, and forecast further weakening.

facts.label: Naming system
facts.value: “Dolphin” is a name contributed by Hong Kong, China, under the ESCAP/WMO Typhoon Committee naming list; it refers to the Chinese white dolphin and a Hong Kong mascot.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the August 8-10 Japan-to-China impact period and preparedness or disruption measures, not Dolphin’s full late-July development, its complete inland dissipation, or all effects elsewhere in the region.

stories.title: Colombian Forces Kill Six Rebels in Military Operation Following New President's Inauguration
stories.summary: In a military operation in Antioquia department, Colombian forces killed six individuals, including four members of a splinter faction of the former FARC guerrilla group and two members of the Gulf Clan drug cartel. This operation occurred shortly after the inauguration of President Abelardo de la Espriella, signaling a strong stance against armed groups in the country.
